title: EGA VI. Plans, notations, problèmes ouverts : notes manuscrites (s.d.).

deep.reconstruction:
This is the last page of a planning dossier for the projected later chapters of EGA (V/VI). It follows a page headed 'Problèmes ouverts' and is titled 'Problèmes-types à résoudre' ('model problems to be solved'). It lists ten problems, labelled a) to j). In the left margin Grothendieck keyed most of them to planned sections (§3,4; §7; §17; §20,21; Chap. VI) or to people (Mumford; Mumford–Seshadri–Narasimhan; Raynaud). Some items are boxed (a, c, j), which may mark priority.

(a) [§7] Rings of definition for structures without automorphisms. If an object over a field or ring has no nontrivial automorphisms, its moduli functor is a sheaf. Descent theory then gives a smallest ring of definition (field of moduli = field of definition) and representability questions become sheaf questions. In modern terms: a rigid stack is an algebraic space.

(b) [§§20,21, Chap. VI] Hilbert and Picard schemes without a projectivity hypothesis, annotated 'partial results'. Also the dual of a non-projective abelian scheme, annotated 'OK by Raynaud'. In FGA, Hilb and Pic were built only for projective morphisms. Removing that hypothesis needs algebraic spaces (Artin 1969) or special arguments (Murre–Oort for Pic over a field). Raynaud (Faisceaux amples sur les schémas en groupes, LNM 119, 1970) settled the dual of an abelian scheme that is not projective.

(c) [§§3,4] Taking quotients without a flatness hypothesis. The quotient of a scheme by an equivalence relation or groupoid, where the projections are not flat. The SGA3/SGA1 results need flatness or a finite group acting on a quasi-projective scheme.

(d) [Mumford] Quotient by a group G acting 'without fixed point', i.e. freely or with trivial stabilisers. This is the setting of Mumford's GIT (1965) for proper free actions. In general the quotient exists only as an algebraic space.

(e) Moduli of 'more or less arbitrary' varieties, with abelian schemes as the case to treat.

(f) [Mumford–Seshadri–Narasimhan, vector bundles; finite case; §17] Classification (moduli) of principal bundles on X/Y with affine structure group G over Y. The cases G commutative and G non-commutative are to be distinguished. For commutative G this is Picard-type (H^1 of a commutative group scheme). For non-commutative G it is non-abelian H^1, i.e. what is now called Bun_G.

(g) Some special case with G finite. G-torsors for finite G are étale or finite covers, which ties the problem to the relative fundamental group.

(h) Particular case X = P^1_Y, G = GL(n), with the marginal query 'Pb mal posé?' ('ill-posed problem?'). Over a field, Grothendieck's 1957 theorem says every bundle on P^1 splits. In families the splitting type jumps, so a fine or separated moduli space cannot exist. The query reflects this.

(i) [Chap. VI, 'Oui'] Is the formal moduli of an abelian variety smooth over the base ring? The answer recorded is yes: deformations of abelian varieties are unobstructed, and the deformation space has g^2 dimensions over W(k).

(j) [boxed] Theorem of the square in a non-projective case, i.e. for abelian schemes or algebraic spaces without an ample line bundle.

The page as a whole is a list of foundational representability and moduli problems that EGA V/VI was supposed to address. Most were later solved by others, notably Artin, Raynaud, Mumford, Oort, Keel–Mori and Kollár.
errors: No mathematical errors. Item (h) is self-flagged as possibly ill-posed. This is correct: families of vector bundles on P^1_Y have jumping splitting type, so no separated or fine moduli space exists. Only a non-separated stack, stratified by splitting type, is available.

deep.surprise_reason: This is a planning list of standard foundational problems of the late 1960s, all of which were later taken up and largely solved (Artin, Raynaud, Oort, Kollár, Keel–Mori). Its interest is historical: it shows how the projected EGA V/VI chapters were organised around these problems, and it records Raynaud's resolution of the non-projective dual. There is no new mathematics.
